SpVgQ4m3m7s.text: Everyone uploading PDFs to Claude is basically wasting their tokens and Microsoft had a free solution to this for months. So every time you upload a PDF, Claude has to process the entire thing. The formatting, the broken tables, the images and all the extra junk inside the file. And each PDF page can consume between 1500 to 3000 tokens. So 20 page document burns through up to 70,000 tokens in one shot. And this is before you even ask your first question. The fix is simple. It's called Marketown, a free Microsoft tool with over 110,000 stars on GitHub. It takes any file, be it PDFs, Word docs, Excel sheets, Powerpoints or even YouTube videos, and converts them into clean Marketown text. This drops your token usage by up to 70%. And Claude actually gives better answers because it was trained on millions of Marketown documents and understands the format natively. Plus, Marketown comes with an MCP server, meaning when you connect it to Claude desktop, it automatically converts every file you upload to a .md file. So check the pinned comment for the tool link and the full PDF guide.

oIJCv4iy_ko.text: Ask Claude Code for a diagram and you usually get this. Default blue boxes, thick arrows, drop shadows. It looks like it was made in 2009. Diagram design has over 44,000 stars on GitHub and it is a free plugin for Claude Code. Here is how it works. The skill gives Claude a proper style guide and a set of strict rules. One accent color per diagram, no shadows, real typography, and a budget for how many boxes and arrows each diagram is allowed. There are 42 types, from architecture and sequence diagrams to state machines, timelines, and even charts. Everything comes out as clean HTML and SVG and it can export PNG at double resolution. The best part is onboarding. You point it at your website, it reads your colors and fonts and writes a style guide that every future diagram uses. Installation is two commands. I send out a free weekly newsletter with the best Claude Code repos I find so you get them before they show up on YouTube. The link is in the description. Here is the demo. I gave Claude code my newsletter website and the Xcalidraw source code and asked for three diagrams explaining how undo and redo actually work. First, it branded itself. It pulled my exact colors from the site, near black ink and my orange accent, plus baby's new way for headings and inter for body text. My site also has a yellow and it deliberately left that out because the rule is one accent color. Then it read the code and planned every diagram against its budget. Nine boxes and 12 arrows for the architecture, five lifelines for the sequence, four states for the stacks. It even chose to leave out some internals to keep them readable. Then it checked its own renders and fixed a loop label sitting on the wrong lifeline and a wrong tag on one of the boxes. And this is what it made. A new edit wipes the redo stack, but just selecting something does not. Then it put all three on one overview page in my brand and opened it in the browser, a few honest things. That run took about 11 minutes. It wrote a Python script to generate the diagrams rather than drawing them by hand and a few commands failed during the brand step, which it worked around on its own. The output is HTML, SVG and PNG, so you cannot drag the boxes around like in Figma. And I have not checked every arrow against the code, so treat it like a first draft from a very fast designer. But for docs, read me's and onboarding new developers going from a code base to diagrams this clean in your own brand is genuinely useful. SkCvYgXETuY.text: What exactly is an AI harness? People talk about models like Claude, GPT or Gemini as if the model itself does everything. It isn't. The model is only one part of the system. The harness is the software around the model that lets it do useful work. And a good example is Claude code. Imagine you ask Claude code to find the bug, fix it, and run the tests. The model can reason about the task, but by itself it cannot open your files. It can't search the repository, run terminal commands, or execute the test suite. Claude code gives it those abilities. So it decides to inspect some files with a structured tool request. Claude code reads the files and puts the result back into the model's context. Now it thinks again and decides the bug is probably in this function. So it asks the harness to edit the file, then run the tests. The harness runs it and the test output comes back into the context. The model sees one test failed, edits the code again and reruns the tests. That loop is the important part. Think, act, observe, think again. The model provides the reasoning. The harness provides the ability to act, but tools are only one part of a harness. It also manages context. Your prompt, history, open files, terminal output, tool results, instructions, all of that must fit inside a limited context window. So the harness decides what stays, what's summarized, what's removed, and what loads again later. That's why the same model can feel smarter in one product than another. The difference might not be the model. It might be the harness. Now add permissions. Maybe it can read files freely, but needs approval before running a dangerous shell command. Maybe it can edit code, but cannot deploy to production without confirmation. The harness controls those boundaries too. And then there's orchestration. Imagine one task has three parts. The back end, the front end, and the tests. A more advanced harness can coordinate sub-agents and bring the results together. Claude is the brain. Claude code gives that brain your repository, terminal, git, tests, tools, context, and the loop that keeps it working. And this is why AI agents are not just models. The model might be brilliant, but without a good harness. It is basically a brain sitting in a jar. Give it tools, memory, permissions, and an environment it can act in. And now you have an agent.
SkCvYgXETuY.title: What Is an AI Harness? Claude Code Explained
